items.reason: Part A now writes its verdict where the change can carry it: scripts/agent-review.mjs gained --annotate (each finding emitted as a GitHub check annotation anchored to file and line, so it renders on the commit and inline on a PR's Files view) and --json (a countable record uploaded beside mechanical.md for 90 days); the judgment job posts Part A's report as the PR comment when no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is configured, so a PR is never left with a bare tick; and a new weekly reporting-rung workflow (.github/workflows/agent-review-history.yml -> scripts/agent-review-history.mjs, npm run review:agent:history) reads those annotations back to report which rubric rules have actually fired, over what, and how often — the question that previously had no answer short of re-running the script commit by commit. Four new assertions in test-unit/delivery-contract.test.mjs (inside check:ci and the pre-push hook) fail if the annotation flag, the JSON record, the 90-day retention, the keyless PR comment, or the history workflow's read-only scopes are removed, so the trail cannot be undone in silence.

The two dangerous-workflow findings are false at HEAD and were already blocked by this repo's own required check (scripts/actions-pin.mjs rules P2/P5, run in sast.yml's workflow-policy job and inside check:ci): sast.yml contains no pull_request_target — only the P2 rule's own prose names it — and every ${{ }} in agent-review.yml lands in an env: block, none in a run: body. Rather than edit prose to placate the scanner I widened the enforcement to the classes it does not yet cover: new blocking rule P7 (an attacker-controlled context — github.event.*, github.head_ref — may appear ONLY as an env: binding, never in run:, with: or if:, which closes the actions/github-script-shaped hole P5 misses) and P8 (container images and docker:// steps must be digest-pinned, the 'container images to a digest' half of the finding). Both pass on all five workflows today, so red is a regression. The pinning half is real and NOT done: every uses: in the repo is first-party, so STRICT=false plus RATCHET.pinned=0 makes the gate green at 0-of-N by exemption. Closing it needs `npm run actions:pin` (a networked run) then STRICT=true and RATCHET.pinned=<count> in the same commit; this session has no network and no shell, and inventing 40-hex SHAs would break every workflow. The script header now spells out those three steps verbatim as the only way to close it.

lessons: systedo-case encodes its own policy as blocking zero-dependency node scripts inside `npm run check:ci` (actions-pin.mjs, merge-gate.mjs, sast.mjs, agent-review.mjs), and those scripts document the hazard in prose that quotes it. Generic YAML scanners flag the prose, so before changing a workflow here, check whether the repo already blocks the pattern — and if the enforcement is real but narrow, widen the rule instead of editing the comment.

A gate can be green by exemption rather than by compliance, and that reads identically from outside. actions-pin.mjs prints '0 of 24 pinned' and exits 0 because first-party actions are exempt and the ratchet floor is 0. When a repo has a ratchet, read its baseline before believing its pass — and when the fix needs network the lane does not have, write the exact three-step command sequence into the file the operator will open, not into a report they will not.

In a repo that ships master on push, the reviewer's trail matters more than its verdict: there is no PR to comment on, so findings have to attach to the commit (check annotations) or they exist only for as long as anyone keeps the run tab open. Annotations are also the only part of a run still queryable afterwards, which is what makes 'which rules have actually been firing' answerable at all.
